elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang for cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies up to March 16, 2023, to conduct a meta-analysis of global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a meta-analysis (systematic review) of the global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate.

elements.quote: However, the trend of reinfection rate over time is not clear. ... to conduct a meta-analysis of global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate.
elements.reason: The abstract states the review objective: to estimate the global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate and its trend over time.

elements.quote: We searched ... for cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies up to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The abstract mentions the study designs sought, but does not explicitly state the main inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., reinfection definition, sample size threshold).

elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang ... up to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The abstract lists the information sources and the date of the last search (March 16, 2023).

elements.quote: The risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the risk-of-bias assessment methods used.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed for age, country, study type, and study population, and time-varying reinfection rates of SARS-CoV-2 were estimated using meta-regression.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis methods: meta-analysis, subgroup analyses, and meta-regression.

elements.quote: A total of 55 studies involving 111,846 cases of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection were included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies (55) and reinfection cases (111,846), but not the total participants and only minimal study characteristics.

elements.quote: The pooled SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate was 0.94% (95% CI : 0.65 -1.35%). In the subgroup analyses, there were statistically significant differences in the pooled reinfection rates by reinfection variant, and study type ( P < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcome (pooled reinfection rate) and subgroup findings.

elements.quote: The pooled SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate was 0.94% (95% CI : 0.65 -1.35%).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports the summary estimate with its 95% confidence interval.

elements.quote: SARS-CoV-2 is at risk of reinfection and the Omicron variant has a higher reinfection rate than other currently known variants.
elements.reason: For subgroup comparisons, the abstract indicates the direction of effect, e.g., Omicron has a higher reinfection rate than other variants.
The abstract does not mention any limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations appear only in the main text.

elements.quote: The results of this study could help guide public health measures and vaccination strategies in response to the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
elements.reason: The abstract's Conclusion provides an interpretation of the time-varying reinfection pattern and its implications for public health and vaccination strategies.
The abstract does not state the funding source; funding is reported only in the main text (text_19).
The abstract does not report the registry name or registration number; PROSPERO registration (CRD42023411778) appears only in the main text (text_6).

elements.quote: There is a significant increase in the number of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection reports in various countries. However, the trend of reinfection rate over time is not clear.
elements.reason: The abstract background describes the current state of knowledge (increasing reinfection reports) and explicitly identifies the key uncertainty (unclear trend of reinfection rate over time); the Introduction (text_4) further describes the global burden and ongoing mutation of SARS-CoV-2.

elements.quote: The results of this study could help guide public health measures and vaccination strategies in response to the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
elements.reason: The need for the review is explained: the unclear time trend of reinfection motivates the meta-analysis, and the Introduction (text_4) emphasizes that SARS-CoV-2 'remains a global health threat,' establishing the review's importance.

elements.quote: the advantage of this study was that compared with the previous meta-analysis of the SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate, first, to avoid the heterogeneous impact of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection definition on SARSCoV-2 reinfection rates
elements.reason: The Discussion acknowledges a previous meta-analysis and explains how the current review improves on it, but the previous review is not identified or cited, and this comparison is not made in the Introduction/rationale section.
This is a review of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rates (etiology/prognosis), not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action needs to be described.
The review does not evaluate complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: Therefore, the aim of this study was to conduct a meta-analysis to describe and summarize the current reinfection rates in different regions and among diverse populations. Furthermore, the study sought to examine trends in reinfection rates over time, so as to provide reference for the development of global unified reinfection standards and reinfection measures in the future.
elements.reason: The objectives are explicitly stated: to meta-analyze current SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rates across regions/populations and to examine time trends in reinfection rates. The title also frames the review question ('How does the SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate change over time?').
This is a review of reinfection rates (frequency estimation) with meta-regression, not a review of intervention effects comparing interventions, so PICO-formatted planned comparisons do not apply.

elements.quote: The inclusion criteria were: (1) Conformed to research questions, i.e., studies that estimated the reinfection rate of SARS-CoV-2 or we could calculate it based on the data provided in the paper; (2) The study design included cohort study, case-control study, and descriptive study; (3) The study fited our working definition of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection... reinfection working definition in this study was based on a positive laboratory result at least 90 days after laboratory confirmation of primary infection
elements.reason: Eligible study designs, the research question (reinfection rate estimation), and the reinfection working definition (≥90 days between positive tests) are explicitly specified.

elements.quote: To avoid language bias, the search was not limited to any language... The exclusion criteria were: ... (4) Grey literature, including a range of documents not controlled by commercial publishing organizations.
elements.reason: Language (no restriction) and publication status (grey literature excluded) are reported, but dissemination year limits are not specified.

elements.quote: One of them reported only the reinfection rate, but not the associated number of first infections as well as the number of reinfections... Therefore, we excluded the above literature with the number of unreported infections
elements.reason: The review does not explicitly distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported; the exclusion reason given conflates data reporting with eligibility.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed for age, reinfection variant, country, study population, and study type respectively
elements.reason: Groups used in the syntheses (age, variant, country, population, study type) are specified and correspond to the review objective of describing reinfection rates across regions and populations and over time.

elements.quote: first, we did not include the 'grey literature', which may lack potential relevant studies that meet the inclusion criteria [35]... In order to avoid data heterogeneity in metaanalysis while ensuring data quantity, we used previous literature and previous definitions of reinfection in some countries as the criteria for included literature
elements.reason: Rationales for notable restrictions (excluding grey literature; adopting the 90-day reinfection definition to limit heterogeneity) are provided.

elements.quote: However, when the rate is close to 0 or 1, two problems will occur in the meta-regression: the confidence interval may exceed the interval of 0-1, and the variance is squeezed towards 0.
